question_text: Identify the sentence that avoids a dangling modifier.

options.text: Having completed the audit, the report was submitted to the Bureau of Internal Revenue.
Having completed the audit, the CPA submitted the report to the Bureau of Internal Revenue.
Walking into the office, the computer was left turned on overnight.
While reviewing the documents, a syntax error was discovered by the clerk.

hint_ladder.title: Look at the Opening Phrase
hint_ladder.text: Sentences that start with an '-ing' phrase (like 'Having completed...' or 'Walking into...') are setting up an action. Your job is to figure out who or what is doing that action.

hint_ladder.title: The Comma Test
hint_ladder.text: Here's the golden rule: whatever noun comes right after the comma must be the one performing the action in the opening phrase. If it can't logically do it, the sentence is broken.

hint_ladder.title: Test Each Option
hint_ladder.text: For option A, ask: can a report complete an audit? No. For option B: can a CPA complete an audit? Yes. For C: can a computer walk into an office? No. For D: can a syntax error review documents? No.

hint_ladder.title: Spot the Only Logical Match
hint_ladder.text: Only one sentence has a subject that can logically perform the action described in the opening phrase. That's your answer.

A.text: This one is tricky because it sounds official. But read it literally: 'Having completed the audit' is describing 'the report.' Reports don't complete audits—people do. The modifier is dangling because the real actor (the person who did the audit) is missing from the sentence.

B.text: This sentence works perfectly. The opening phrase 'Having completed the audit' naturally attaches to 'the CPA'—a person who can logically finish an audit. The modifier is properly anchored to its subject.

C.text: This one is almost funny if you picture it: 'Walking into the office' is supposed to describe 'the computer.' But computers don't walk. The real person who walked into the office is never named, so the modifier just hangs there, unattached.

D.text: This sentence has a similar problem. 'While reviewing the documents' is meant to describe whoever was doing the reviewing, but the subject that follows is 'a syntax error.' Errors don't review anything—people do. The clerk is mentioned later, but it's too late; the modifier is already dangling.

next_time_rule: When you see an '-ing' phrase at the start of a sentence, immediately check the noun right after the comma. That noun must be the one doing the action. If it can't, the sentence has a dangling modifier.
blueprint_id: Dangling Modifiers — Aligning Introductory Participle with Logical Subject
deconstruct_text:
Let me walk you through how to think about this one, because dangling modifiers are a classic exam trap.

First, notice that all four sentences start with an introductory phrase that describes an action: 'Having completed the audit,' 'Walking into the office,' or 'While reviewing the documents.' These phrases are like arrows pointing to whoever is doing the action. The problem is, in three of these sentences, the arrow points to the wrong target.

Here's the simple trick: whatever comes immediately after the comma must be the one performing the action in the opening phrase. Let's test each one:

Option A: 'Having completed the audit, the report...' Can a report complete an audit? No. The arrow points to 'the report,' but that doesn't make sense. The real actor (the person who did the audit) is missing.

Option B: 'Having completed the audit, the CPA...' Can a CPA complete an audit? Absolutely. The arrow lands on the right target. This one is correct.

Option C: 'Walking into the office, the computer...' Can a computer walk? No. The arrow points to something that can't possibly do the action.

Option D: 'While reviewing the documents, a syntax error...' Can an error review documents? No. The arrow is pointing at the wrong thing again.

The mental framework here is simple: think of the introductory phrase as a spotlight. Whatever noun steps into that spotlight right after the comma must be the one doing the action. If it can't logically do it, the sentence is broken. Only option B passes this test.
